passage:
A year ago I was the person up at 3 a.m. posting about how the whole town's problems were someone else's fault. I lost two friends. I nearly lost Usha, who'd been my friend since Class 4.
The way back wasn't one moment. First I deleted the apps from my phone for a month. Just that. I started sleeping. Then my mother found me a counsellor at the district hospital, and I went every Thursday. I talked about the job I didn't get, and the shame of it.
The anger didn't go away. Our town really had been ignored: no bus route, no jobs. That part was true. What I let go of was hating people for it.
Now I help run a residents' group. We've filed petitions for the bus route and got two meetings with the council. Usha comes on Saturdays. Last week the route got approved.
I'm still angry. It just builds things now.
— Vishal

qa.a: They filed petitions for the bus route.

qa.a: Deleting the apps, sleeping, seeing a counsellor and joining lawful local action gave the real grievance a useful outlet without the hatred.

qa.q: What is it like for Usha to come on Saturdays now?
qa.a: Usha probably feels relieved and glad to have that friendship back, working on something good together.

Counsellor's note, month six. Written by Rajni.
Imran (24) first came in after his family found his posts. He hadn't slept properly in months and was furious about the leaked recruitment exam that had cost him two years. The anger was about something real.
What's changed: he took the social apps off his phone in month two. He sleeps about seven hours most nights now, he says. He has stopped using the ugly word he once used for a whole community he blamed. He brought it up himself, embarrassed.
He has joined a lawful student group filing complaints about exam leaks, and on Sundays he tutors four boys from his lane for the same exam, for free.
Today he said, 'I'm still angry about the leak. I'm just not angry at a people any more.'
Next: move to monthly sessions. Check in about the exam results in March, which may stir things up.

qa.q: How many boys does Imran tutor on Sundays?
qa.a: He tutors four boys from his lane.

qa.q: What does Imran's embarrassment about his old word for a whole community show?
qa.a: It shows he now feels ashamed of the hatred and has let it go, while still caring about the injustice.

qa.q: What did Imran do that turned his anger into something useful?
qa.a: He stepped back from social apps, slept, kept up counselling, joined a lawful group filing complaints and tutored others, directing anger at the problem, not at people.

qa.q: How might the four boys Imran tutors be affected by his change?
qa.a: They get free help and a model of someone who turned anger about unfairness into practical support.

grounding: It shows a young man stepping back from feeds, sleeping, seeing a counsellor and channelling a real grievance into lawful action and teaching, while dropping hatred.

passage:
Monday night
Eight weeks off the forums today. I deleted the apps in March, when I couldn't remember the last time I'd slept more than five hours.
I still get angry. The landfill fire near our colony is real. The kids in our lane really do cough all winter. Elizabeth, my counsellor, said something today that stuck: "Your anger about the landfill is valid. Hating people online never put out a single fire."
So this week I did something boring instead. I wrote a complaint to the municipal office with twenty-three signatures from our lane. I joined the ward residents' meeting. I read the pollution board's report, all forty pages, with a highlighter.
Nobody liked or shared any of it. But on Saturday an officer actually came to see the site.
I sleep seven hours now. I still care. I just don't hate anymore.
Salma

qa.q: How many signatures did the complaint have?
qa.a: Twenty-three signatures from our lane.

qa.q: How does Salma seem to feel eight weeks off the forums?
qa.a: Salma feels calmer and rested, still angry about the landfill but no longer consumed by hatred.

qa.q: What turned Salma's anger into something useful?
qa.a: Lawful, concrete steps: a signed complaint, joining the residents' meeting and reading the report, alongside counselling and sleep.

qa.q: How might the families in Salma's lane feel about the complaint?
qa.a: They likely feel hopeful and supported, seeing someone take their children's coughing to the officials.

passage:
For a year Lalremsiami had spent nights raging online about the road to her village near Champhai. The contractors had taken the money, the monsoon had taken the road, and the posts she read blamed whole groups of people for it. She had begun to hate faces she'd never met.
In spring she stopped. She handed her phone to her mother every night at nine. She slept. She talked twice with the counsellor at the district hospital.
The anger stayed, but she aimed it. With Tushar, the young schoolteacher, she walked the road with a notebook and photographed every broken stretch. They collected forty-one signatures and took the file to the village council, then to the block office, politely, twice.
In October a survey team came. Nothing was fixed yet. But when Tushar asked if she was still angry, she said, "Yes. At the road. Not at people."

qa.q: How many signatures did they collect?
qa.a: Forty-one signatures.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami mean by 'At the road. Not at people'?
qa.a: She still feels angry about the injustice, but calmer, having let go of hatred for people she had never met.

qa.q: Which steps helped her redirect the anger?
qa.a: Giving up the phone at night, sleeping, seeing a counsellor, and lawful action: documenting the road and taking signatures to the council and block office.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Lalremsiami's change?
qa.a: Tushar likely sees a determined, steady partner and feels encouraged working beside her.

grounding: A young woman in a village steps back from rage feeds, sleeps, sees a counsellor and turns her grievance into lawful local action.

passage: The rents in Aiko's Osaka neighbourhood had doubled in three years, and for most of last winter she had spent every night reading threads that blamed newcomers for it, reply after furious reply. In March she deleted the forum app. It was harder than she expected. Her friend Sofia, who lived two streets away, came with her to the ward office's free counselling hour, and the counsellor asked what Aiko wanted to change, not just who she hated. By May, Aiko was sleeping seven hours. She joined the local tenants' group that met in the community hall on Thursdays and learned how rent rules actually worked. At the June meeting, she sat beside a family who had moved in last year and were facing the same increase. They split the work of writing a joint letter to the landlord. Aiko was still angry. It just pointed somewhere useful now.

qa.q: Where did the tenants' group meet?
qa.a: The tenants' group met in the community hall on Thursdays.

qa.q: How does Aiko feel by the June meeting?
qa.a: She is still angry about the rents but steadier and more hopeful, because her anger now has a useful direction.

qa.q: Which steps helped Aiko turn her anger into something useful?
qa.a: Deleting the forum app, going to counselling with Sofia, sleeping properly and joining the tenants' group all shifted her anger from people to a real problem.

qa.q: How might the family who moved in last year see Aiko at the meeting?
qa.a: They likely see a neighbour facing the same increase and working beside them, not someone who once blamed people like them.

grounding: Shows a person stepping back from feeds, sleeping, seeing a counsellor and channelling a real grievance into lawful local action while dropping hatred of people.
